en: The Noble Sūtra on Impermanence. Om, homage to the Omniscient One!

Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery, together with a great saṅgha of monks, numbering twelve hundred and fifty monks.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Monks, all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, unstable, unreliable, and subject to change.
Therefore, monks, it is enough to turn away from all conditioned phenomena; it is enough to become dispassionate toward them; it is enough to be liberated from them."

For all beings, for all creatures, for all living things, life indeed ends with death; death is its finality. There is no such thing as non-death for one who is born. Even those householders, monks, who belong to great śāla families of brahmins, great śāla families of kṣatriyas, or great śāla families of vaiśyas—those who possess vast wealth and great enjoyments, with abundant collections of gems, rubies, pearls, beryl, conch shells, crystals, coral, gold, and silver—even they [must face this].

Those who possess vast accumulations of wealth, grain, treasuries, and granaries; those who have many female and male slaves, laborers, and servants; and those who have many friends, ministers, kinsmen, and blood relations—even for them, life ends in death and concludes with death.
There is no such thing as non-death for one who is born.

Furthermore, O monks, even those kings who are Kṣatriyas, consecrated upon the crown of the head, who have attained sovereignty, power, and heroism over the countryside, and who dwell having conquered a great circle of the earth—[for them too, life ends in death].
For even their life ends in death; death is its conclusion. There is no such thing as non-death for one who is born.

Even those monks, O bhikṣus, who are seers living as forest-dwellers, subsisting on fallen fruit, eating fallen fruit, and maintaining themselves with fallen fruit—even for them, life ends in death; death is its conclusion. There is no such thing as non-death for one who is born.

O monks, even those gods of the desire realm—the Cāturmahārājika gods, the Trāyastriṃśa gods, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods—even for them, life ends in death;
death is the finality of existence. There is no such thing as non-death for one who is born.

O monks, even those form-realm gods who have attained the first dhyāna—the Brahmakāyika, Brahmāpurohita, and Mahābrahmā gods; and those who have attained the second dhyāna—the Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, and Ābhāsvara gods—[for them too, life ends in death].

For those who have attained the third dhyāna—the Parīttaśubhas, Apramāṇaśubhas, and Śubhakṛtsnas—and for those who have attained the fourth dhyāna—the Anabhrakas, Puṇyaprasavas, Bṛhatphalas, Avṛhas, Atapas, Sudṛśas, Sudarśanas, and Akaniṣṭha devas—even for them, life ends in death; death is their finality. There is no non-death for one who is born. And as for those monks, the formless devas—those who have reached the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—for them too [it is the same].
Life ends in death; death is its finality. For one who is born, there is no non-death.
This is the triple world.

Even those monks who are arhats—whose taints are exhausted, who have accomplished their task, performed what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained their own goal, whose fetters of existence are completely destroyed, and whose minds are well-liberated through right knowledge—even they [are subject to this].
Even for those who have attained the supreme perfection of mastery over all mental states, there is the nature of laying down the body.

And as for those monks who are Pratyekabuddhas, like the horn of a rhinoceros, who tame themselves alone, pacify themselves alone, and attain final Nirvāṇa by themselves—even for them, this is the nature of laying down the body. And as for those monks who are Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, endowed with the power of the ten strengths, possessing noble majesty, uttering the perfect lion’s roar, and having ascended to the fearlessness of the four grounds of self-confidence—[for them too, it is the same].

The fearlessness of teaching all dharmas, the fearlessness of leading others onto the path to nirvāṇa, and the fearlessness of the knowledge that has abandoned the outflows (*āsrava*). Even those whose bodies are as firm and solid as the *nārāyaṇa* strength possess this nature of having their bodies cast down. Just as, monks, vessels made by a potter—whether unbaked or baked—are destined for breaking and end in breaking, even so, monks, it is with all sentient beings.
For all beings, for all living creatures, life indeed ends with death; it culminates in death. There is no non-death for one who is born.
Thus spoke the Blessed One; having spoken this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further said: "Impermanent, alas, are conditioned phenomena; their nature is arising and passing away."
They arise and pass away; their subsiding is bliss.
Just as a clay vessel made by a potter ends inevitably in breakage, so too does the life of sentient beings end in death.
Just as ripe fruits are constantly in danger of falling,
so too are sentient beings born of their formative predispositions always in danger of death.
All accumulations end in depletion; all elevations end in a fall;
all unions end in separation; indeed, life ends in death.
Thus spoke the Blessed One; and those monks and that entire assembly, with joyful minds, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
Thus ends the noble *Anityatā-sūtra*.
